name: krb5_ret_creds_tag
prose: Reads a tagged credentials record from the storage sp into creds (store.c:1520-1591; the real name is krb5_ret_creds_tag, the packet slice held only its tail). It zeroes *creds, reads a 32-bit header whose bits say which optional parts follow, and then reads in order: the client principal if SC_CLIENT_PRINCIPAL is set, the server principal if SC_SERVER_PRINCIPAL, the session keyblock if SC_SESSION_KEY, always the times, always an 8-bit dummy and a 32-bit flags word, then the addresses if SC_ADDRESSES, the authdata if SC_AUTHDATA, the ticket if SC_TICKET and the second ticket if SC_SECOND_TICKET. The flags word is bit-swapped with bitswap32 when it has bits set in a mask chosen from the native layout of the flags union, and is stored in creds->flags.i. Any failing read goes to the cleanup label, which returns that error code at once with *creds partly filled in; the code to free it is compiled out (#if 0), so nothing is freed and the caller owns whatever was already allocated. On success it returns 0; the optional fields whose header bit was not set are left zeroed, not decoded.
note: store.c:1519-1591 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer right: the optional fields are decoded only when their header bits are set (1532-1582), so the old statement that all fields are decoded on success was wrong.

name: _krb5_extract_ticket
prose: Processes a decoded KDC reply and fills creds (ticket.c:649-850; the real name is _krb5_extract_ticket and the earlier "unnamed" label described its tail). Arguments include the reply rep, the credentials creds, a key and usage, optional addresses addrs, the expected nonce, extraction flags and an optional decrypt procedure (default decrypt_tkt). It decrypts the encrypted part (an error goes to the out label), copies the session key into creds->session (failure to out), converts the reply's client name and checks it against creds->client with check_client_referral unless EXTRACT_TICKET_ALLOW_CNAME_MISMATCH is set, replacing creds->client with the reply's principal, and does the same for the server with check_server_referral unless EXTRACT_TICKET_ALLOW_SERVER_MISMATCH is set. With EXTRACT_TICKET_MATCH_REALM it requires the reply's server realm to equal both the server's and the client's realm (else KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED). It requires the nonce to match (else KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED). It optionally adjusts context->kdc_sec_offset for an initial ticket when time sync is requested. Time checks: with creds->times.starttime equal to 0 a reply start time (or authtime) more than context->max_skew from now gives KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW; a non-zero preset starttime that differs from the reply's gives KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED, as do a reply renew_till larger than a non-zero preset one and a reply endtime larger than a non-zero preset one. It then stores starttime, renew_till, authtime and endtime in creds->times, copies the addresses from the reply, else from addrs, else leaves them empty (the result of krb5_copy_addresses is ignored), copies the flags, clears authdata, ASN.1-encodes the ticket into creds->ticket (an encoding error goes to out; a length mismatch aborts through krb5_abortx) and clears second_ticket. The out label zeroes rep->enc_part.key.keyvalue.data over its length on every path, including failures, and the function returns ret.
note: Partly read: ticket.c:645-850 (comments skipped); the first lines 660-695 and 745-850 were read in full, check_client_referral, check_server_referral and decrypt_tkt were not. The old prose said errors come from krb5_copy_addresses, which is wrong because its result is ignored at lines 823 and 825; the early-return behaviour and the zeroing at 846-849 apply to all paths.

name: make_path
prose: Static helper in transited.c (lines 62-128) that inserts the intermediate realms between from and to into the singly linked list after node r (r->realm itself is not changed). It first swaps from and to if from is the shorter string. If to is a suffix of from (the strcmp at line 75), it repeatedly finds the next '.' in the text starting at from; if there is none it clears the context error message and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY; otherwise it steps past the '.', stops when the remainder equals to, and else calls calloc for a node, inserts it right after r (newest node first) and strdups the remainder into it. If to is instead a prefix of from (strncmp over strlen(to)), it starts at the end of from and in a loop scans backwards for '/' (the scan can run below from when from contains no '/', which is not guarded: only a stop exactly at from returns KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY, and that return does not clear the error message), stops when the first p - from characters of to equal those of from, and otherwise inserts a node holding a malloc'd copy of from up to p and continues with p decremented. If neither relation holds it clears the error message and returns KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY. It returns 0 on success. A calloc failure returns krb5_enomem(context) with the new node never linked; a strdup or malloc failure unlinks and frees that node and returns krb5_enomem; nodes inserted by earlier iterations remain linked after r, and the function never frees r or other pre-existing nodes.
note: transited.c:61-128 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (a failure after partial insertion leaves earlier new nodes linked); reviewer 2 right (without a '/' the backward scan passes below from instead of returning KRB5KDC_ERR_POLICY, 101-103); reviewer 3 right (the precondition needs from to start with '/' or the scan goes before the buffer).

name: getopt
prose: Roken's BSD-style getopt (getopt.c:57-124) using the globals optind, optreset, optopt, opterr, optarg and a function-static scan pointer place. When optreset is set or place is at the end of the current word it starts a new word: it returns -1 (with place reset, without touching optopt) if optind >= nargc or nargv[optind] does not begin with '-'; if the word begins with "--" (any word whose first two characters are '-', not only exactly "--") it advances optind by one and returns -1 without touching optopt. Otherwise it takes the next character as the option, storing it in optopt. If that character is ':' or does not occur in ostr: when it is '-' (for example a lone "-") it returns -1 with optopt '-' and optind unchanged; otherwise it advances optind when that was the last character of the word, prints "illegal option" to stderr when opterr is non-zero and ostr does not start with ':' (using the base name of nargv[0]), and returns '?'. If the option takes no argument (the letter in ostr is not followed by ':') it sets optarg to NULL, advances optind when the word is finished, and returns the character. If it takes an argument: an attached remainder of the word becomes optarg; otherwise, if the next word does not exist (optind has already been incremented by the test) it resets place and returns ':' when ostr starts with ':' or else prints "option requires an argument" when opterr is non-zero and returns '?'; if the next word exists it becomes optarg. After an accepted argument it resets place and advances optind past the consumed word. On the error returns optarg is not modified. The function allocates nothing and takes no locks.
note: getopt.c:57-124 read in full. Reviewer 1 right ('-' not in ostr returns -1, 82-83); reviewer 2 right (the -1 returns at 66-73 happen before optopt is assigned at 76); reviewer 3 right (the "--" test at 70 applies to any word starting with two dashes).

name: main
prose: Test driver of roken's snprintf test (snprintf-test.c:251-264); argc and argv are unused. It starts ret at 0 and adds the return values of cmp_with_sprintf_int(), cmp_with_sprintf_long(), cmp_with_sprintf_long_long() (only when HAVE_LONG_LONG is defined), test_null() and test_sizet(), then returns the sum. Those helpers accumulate the result of the helper try(), which is a strcmp of the rk_vsnprintf output against vsprintf and so can be negative as well as positive, hence a non-zero return of an individual test can cancel against another and the sum can be 0 although a test returned non-zero. The helpers can also end the process with errx(1, "increase buf and try again") when a formatted result does not fit their 256-byte buffer; they print "failed: ..." lines to stdout for mismatches. main itself allocates nothing and takes no locks.
note: snprintf-test.c:34-57 and 250-264 read, with the return statements of the helpers checked by grep. Reviewer right: the sum can be zero with non-zero parts because try() returns strcmp results (56), so "0 exactly when every test returned 0" does not hold.

name: convert_in_un_remote
prose: Static helper in socket_wrapper.c (lines 340-436) that maps the remote IP address inaddr of socket si to a Unix socket path in un->sun_path; bcast may be NULL. It sets *bcast to 0 first. For AF_INET it classifies the host-order address: for a UDP socket 255.255.255.255 gives is_bcast 2 and 127.255.255.255 gives is_bcast 1 (both with the default interface); any address of the form 127.0.0.x gives is_bcast 0 with interface x (only the last byte, not all of 127.0.0.0/8); every other address, including 127.255.255.255 on a non-UDP socket, sets errno to ENETUNREACH and returns -1. For AF_INET it then stores is_bcast in *bcast (before the port test). For AF_INET6 it uses the v6 type character and the fixed interface SW_IPV6_ADDRESS and leaves *bcast at 0; any other family sets ENETUNREACH and returns -1. A port of 0 sets errno EINVAL and returns -1. If is_bcast is non-zero it writes "<socket_wrapper_dir()>/EINVAL" into un->sun_path and returns 0; otherwise it writes "<dir>/" followed by the type character, interface and port encoded with SOCKET_FORMAT and returns 0. The type character stays NUL when si->type is neither SOCK_STREAM nor SOCK_DGRAM.
note: socket_wrapper.c:340-436 read in full. Reviewer 1 and 2 right (127.255.255.255 on a non-UDP socket returns ENETUNREACH, 376 and 386-388; *bcast is set before the port check, 390); reviewer 3 right (only 127.0.0.x is accepted: (addr & 0xFFFFFF00) == 0x7F000000, 381).

name: convert_in_un_alloc
prose: Static helper in socket_wrapper.c (lines 438-544) that maps the local address inaddr of socket si to a Unix socket path in un->sun_path, allocating a port when it is 0; bcast may be NULL. It sets *bcast to 0 first. For AF_INET it classifies the host-order address: 0.0.0.0 gives the default interface with the TCP or UDP type; for a UDP socket 255.255.255.255 gives is_bcast 2 and 127.255.255.255 gives is_bcast 1 (default interface); 127.0.0.x gives interface x (only that /24, not all of 127.0.0.0/8); anything else, including 127.255.255.255 on a non-UDP socket, sets errno EADDRNOTAVAIL and returns -1. For AF_INET6 it uses the v6 type character and interface SW_IPV6_ADDRESS without checking the address; any other family sets ENETUNREACH and returns -1. After the switch it stores is_bcast in *bcast. If the port is 0 it loops prt from 5001 to 9999, builds the candidate path for each, skips ports whose path already exists (stat succeeds) and calls set_port(si->family, prt, si->myname) for the others; the loop has no break, so it keeps going and prt ends at 10000, and that value is then used in the final path. Finally it writes "<socket_wrapper_dir()>/" followed by the type character, interface and port to un->sun_path (also for broadcast addresses, unlike convert_in_un_remote) and returns 0. The type character is NUL when si->type is neither SOCK_STREAM nor SOCK_DGRAM.
note: socket_wrapper.c:438-544 read in full. Reviewer 1 right (0.0.0.0 gets a normal type and interface, 474-478); reviewer 2 right (127.255.255.255 on non-UDP gives EADDRNOTAVAIL, 484 and 494-496); reviewer 3 right (only 127.0.0.x accepted, 489).

name: strftime
prose: Roken's replacement strftime (strftime.c:169-397; the slice held its body and the name strftime_like_format does not exist in the source). Parameters are buf, maxsize, a format string and a struct tm. It loops while the format is not at its end and n < maxsize. A literal character is copied to *buf and n is incremented without any other check. A '%' (optionally followed by an E or O modifier, which is skipped) selects a conversion that is written with snprintf(buf, maxsize - n, ...) from the tm fields and tables (weekday and month names, am/pm, numeric fields, %z from tm_gmtoff or timezone, %Z from tm_zone or tzname); %s calls mktime on the (const-cast) tm, which can modify it; two conversions call abort() (lines 235 and 238); a '%' followed by NUL outputs "%" and the loop then ends, "%%" outputs "%", and an unknown conversion character outputs "%" followed by that character. After each conversion, if snprintf returned a negative value or a length that does not fit in the remaining maxsize - n bytes the function returns 0 at once (in the truncation case snprintf has already written a NUL terminator inside the remaining space, so buf is NUL-terminated up to what it wrote), otherwise it advances buf and n by the length. At the end it writes a NUL at *buf and returns n, the number of characters written excluding the NUL. If literal characters filled maxsize bytes, the final NUL is written one byte past maxsize, so buf must have room for maxsize + 1 bytes in that case.
note: strftime.c:169-397 read; the individual conversion cases 182-340 were checked only with a grep for the snprintf, abort and mktime calls. Reviewer right: on truncation snprintf itself NUL-terminates within the remaining space (385-386), so the old claim that buf is not NUL-terminated was wrong. Fixed under the real name strftime; the packet marked it dropped.

name: yysyntax_error
prose: Bison-generated helper (slc-gram.c:924-1030) that builds a verbose syntax-error message for the token yychar in parser state yystate. It reads yyn = yypact[yystate]; unless YYPACT_NINF < yyn and yyn <= YYLAST it returns 0 (meaning an ordinary "syntax error" message is enough), so it also returns 0 when yyn is above YYLAST. Otherwise it computes the name length of the unexpected token (yytname[YYTRANSLATE(yychar)]) and builds the message format "syntax error, unexpected %s" followed by ", expecting %s" and " or %s" parts for each token name found in yycheck at positions yyn + yyx; if there would be five or more arguments (more than four expected tokens) it discards the expected tokens and keeps only the unexpected one. It sums the name lengths with the format length (yystrlen of the format, in which every %s counts as two characters) with overflow checks and returns YYSIZE_MAXIMUM if the sum overflows. Otherwise, when yyresult is non-NULL it copies the format into yyresult substituting each %s with the corresponding yyarg token name (a NUL-terminated string); with yyresult NULL it writes nothing. The returned value is the computed size, an upper bound that is larger than the actual message length plus NUL by two bytes for each %s placeholder used (that is, by 2 * (1 + number of expected-token names included)), not the exact byte count.
note: slc-gram.c:915-1010 read; the tail of the copy loop (1010-1030) was not read. Reviewer 1 right (size overestimates), reviewer 2 right (the overestimate is 2 per %s including the unexpected token, so it is off by 2 when there are no expected tokens), reviewer 3 right (the return 0 condition is !(YYPACT_NINF < yyn && yyn <= YYLAST), 929-930).

name: WaitAndIncrementThreadCounter
prose: Windows-only helper of the sample GSS server (gss-server.c:594-616) that waits until a worker slot is free and takes it; it takes no arguments and uses the globals hMutex, hEvent, thread_count and max_threads. In an endless loop it waits on hMutex with INFINITE timeout. If that wait returns WAIT_OBJECT_0 and thread_count < max_threads it increments thread_count by one, releases the mutex (the ReleaseMutex result is not checked) and returns TRUE. If thread_count is not below max_threads it releases the mutex and waits on hEvent; if that wait returns WAIT_OBJECT_0 the loop starts again, otherwise it returns FALSE with thread_count unchanged and the mutex released. If the hMutex wait returns anything other than WAIT_OBJECT_0 it returns FALSE without releasing the mutex: for WAIT_FAILED the mutex is not held, but for WAIT_ABANDONED the calling thread has been given ownership and still holds it when the function returns FALSE. On TRUE, thread_count is its old value plus one.
note: gss-server.c:594-616 read in full. Reviewer 1 and 2 right in that the earlier formal contract was weaker than the prose (now empty); reviewer 3 right (WAIT_ABANDONED returns FALSE at 612-613 with the mutex held, so "no mutex held" was not always true).

name: ccs_cache_collection_handle_message
prose: Dispatches one request message for the CCAPI server's cache collection (ccs_cache_collection.c:1010-1109; the real name is ccs_cache_collection_handle_message). It starts with err = 0 and will_block = 0. It sets err to ccErrBadParam if either pipe is invalid or io_cache_collection, in_request_data, out_will_block or out_reply_data is NULL; if no error so far it creates a reply stream with krb5int_ipc_stream_new. Then, for the message id in_request_name, it calls the matching handler: the old release message does nothing (empty reply), and sync, get_change_time, wait_for_change (which can set will_block), get_default_ccache_name, open_ccache, open_default_ccache, create_ccache, create_default_ccache, create_new_ccache, new_ccache_iterator, lock (which can set will_block) and unlock go to their ccs_cache_collection_* functions with the request data and the reply stream; any other id sets ccErrBadInternalMessage. If err is still 0 it stores will_block in *out_will_block and, when will_block is 0, hands the reply stream to the caller in *out_reply_data (the caller must release it), or, when will_block is non-zero, sets *out_reply_data to NULL. In every case the function releases the reply stream if it still owns it (that is, on all errors and in the will-block case) and returns cci_check_error(err), the error code. On an error return *out_will_block and *out_reply_data are not written.
note: ccs_cache_collection.c:1008-1109 read in full. The packet name was wrong (the packet called it an unnamed excerpt); the function exists and is fixed under its real name. No reviewer claim beyond the mechanical name rejection.

name: check_once_cc_context_open_default_ccache
prose: Test helper in the CCAPI test suite (test_ccapi_context.c:498-549) that calls cc_context_open_default_ccache once and checks the outcome; the arguments are a context, an optional pointer to a ccache variable, the expected error code and a description. Inside BEGIN_CHECK_ONCE/END_CHECK_ONCE (not read) and only when the cc_context_open_default_ccache API is defined (otherwise it does nothing and returns 0), it calls cc_context_open_default_ccache(context, ccache), or with NULL when ccache is NULL, and checks the returned error against expected_err and the list of five possible codes with check_err. If the call returned 0 it checks that *ccache is not NULL, reads the opened cache's name with cc_ccache_get_name and the default name with cc_context_get_default_ccache_name (the first result is overwritten by the second, so err ends up as the result of cc_context_get_default_ccache_name), records a test failure if both names exist and differ, releases any obtained name strings, and then, if *ccache is non-NULL, releases the ccache and sets *ccache to NULL, whether or not the verification calls failed. The function returns err: the error of the open call when that failed (with *ccache not modified), otherwise the result of cc_context_get_default_ccache_name. Failures of cc_ccache_get_name or name mismatches are recorded as test failures, not returned.

Reviewer right: after a successful open the ccache is always released and *ccache is set to NULL (538-541), even if a verification call failed, so the old claim that it remains for the caller was wrong. Fixed under the real name; the packet slice cut the head.

name: k5_kinit
prose: Static function of the MIT kinit client (kinit.c:639-852) that obtains, validates or renews credentials according to opts->action (INIT_PW, INIT_KT, VALIDATE, RENEW) using the context, principal k5->me and output cache k5->out_cc from k5. It returns 1 if it reached the point after the credentials were obtained (and, for VALIDATE and RENEW, stored) and 0 otherwise. It allocates init-cred options (failure goes to cleanup silently), sets lifetime, renew life, forwardable, proxiable, canonicalize, anonymous, address list (from krb5_os_localaddr; failure prints a message and goes to cleanup), armor ccache and PAC options, and resolves the keytab for INIT_KT (a KDB: keytab first sets up the KDB; failures print a message through com_err and go to cleanup), sets any pre-authentication options (failure prints and goes to cleanup), and sets the in-ccache and out-ccache on the options (these two failures go to cleanup without printing anything). It then calls the matching krb5 routine for the action; on failure it prints either "Password incorrect while ..." (for KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BAD_INTEGRITY, or a preauth failure after a password prompt) or a com_err message and goes to cleanup. For VALIDATE and RENEW it creates a temporary MEMORY cache, initialises it, stores the credentials and moves it into k5->out_cc (each failure prints and goes to cleanup); on success the temporary cache pointer is cleared. It then sets the success flag (notix = 0) and, if k5->switch_to_cache is set, calls krb5_cc_switch; if that fails it prints an error and goes to cleanup, but since the flag is already set the function still returns 1. Cleanup tears down the KDB keytab state (non-Windows), destroys the temporary MEMORY cache if it was not moved, frees the options object, avoids freeing k5->me through the credentials, frees and clears opts->pa_opts, frees the credential contents and closes the keytab; the address list obtained from krb5_os_localaddr is not freed in the code shown.
note: kinit.c:639-852 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer 1 right (set_in_ccache and set_out_ccache failures go to cleanup silently, 741-746); reviewers 2 and 3 wrong: notix is set to 0 at line 824 before krb5_cc_switch, so a switch failure at 826-830 still ends with return notix ? 0 : 1 equal to 1 (851).

name: get_best_princ_for_target
prose: ksu helper (heuristic.c:505-740; the real name is get_best_princ_for_target, lower case) that chooses the Kerberos principal ksu should use as the client for switching to target_user. It sets *path_out to 0 and returns 0 immediately if *client is already non-NULL. It reads the default principal of cc_source if that cache is initialised (failure goes to cleanup), and parses target_user and source_user into principals (failures to cleanup). If source_uid is 0 it sets *client to the target principal when target_uid is non-zero, else to the cache's default principal if there is one, else to the target principal, and finishes; if source_uid is non-zero and equals target_uid it sets *client to the default principal if present, else to the target principal, and finishes. Otherwise it calls krb5_seteuid(0) and then krb5_seteuid(target_uid); if either fails it returns errno (the effective uid is then unchanged if the first call failed, or 0 if the second failed; the function never restores it on any path, so on the later paths the effective uid stays target_uid). If neither the .k5login nor the .k5users file can be stat'ed it sets *client to the target principal, sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED only when cmd is non-NULL, and returns 0. Otherwise it reads the authorized principal list (an error returns that error); an empty list sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED, leaves *client unchanged and returns 0. It then builds the service principal for hostname and tries three candidate principals in order (the cache's default, the target, the source), looking each up in the list and, when listed, checking for a ticket (find_either_ticket); the first with a ticket is copied into *client and the function finishes. Next it tries each listed principal for an existing ticket and stores the first found in *client. Then it falls back to the first candidate that was merely found in the list and copies it into *client; with PRINC_LOOK_AHEAD compiled in it also tries the closest listed principal to each candidate. If none works it sets *path_out to NOT_AUTHORIZED and returns 0 with *client unchanged. Any intermediate error returns its code, and in all cases the temporary principals are freed; a principal stored in *client is owned by the caller.
note: heuristic.c:505-740 read with the debug printf lines skipped. Reviewer 1 right (the NOT_AUTHORIZED paths return 0 with *client unchanged, 601-606 and 730-731); reviewer 2 right (a failure of the first krb5_seteuid(0) leaves the effective uid unchanged, 578-581).

name: k5_htonll
prose: Static inline function in k5-platform.h (lines 776-786) that converts a 64-bit host-order value to big-endian (network) order. Its body is chosen at compile time: when K5_BE is defined it returns val unchanged; when K5_LE and SWAP64 are defined it returns SWAP64(val), the byte-swapped value; in any other configuration it returns load_64_be applied to the bytes of its local copy of val, which reads the object's bytes as a big-endian number (equal to val on a big-endian host and byte-reversed on a little-endian host). It has no side effects and takes no locks.
note: k5-platform.h:776-786 and load_64_be (634-645) read. The earlier contract allowed either outcome and was weaker than the prose (reviewer right), so it is left empty because the result depends on the build's byte order.

name: k5_ntohll
prose: Static inline function in k5-platform.h (lines 787-791) that converts a 64-bit big-endian (network) order value to host order. It returns k5_htonll(val) (the comment notes the two swaps are identical), so the value is unchanged on a big-endian build (K5_BE) and byte-reversed on a little-endian build with SWAP64, or loaded through load_64_be otherwise. It has no side effects and takes no locks.
note: k5-platform.h:787-791 read in full. The earlier contract allowed either result on any build (reviewer right), so it is left empty because the result depends on the build's byte order.

name: process_tl_data
prose: Static reader in kadmin's dump.c (lines 565-594) that fills the tagged-data nodes of a principal being loaded from a dump file; fname and lineno are used only in messages, filep is the open stream and tl_data the list of preallocated krb5_tl_data nodes. For each node in list order it reads "type<TAB>length<TAB>" with fscanf; if two values are not read it calls load_err and returns EINVAL; if the type is outside INT16_MIN..INT16_MAX or the length is above UINT16_MAX it calls load_err and returns EINVAL. Otherwise it stores the type and length in the node and calls read_octets_or_minus1 to read the contents into tl_data_contents; if that fails it calls load_err and returns EINVAL. It returns 0 after all nodes were processed (also for an empty list). On a failure the nodes before the failing one are complete, the failing node may already have its type and length set (when the failure is in the contents read) and its contents pointer is whatever read_octets_or_minus1 left, and later nodes are untouched.
note: dump.c:565-594 read in full. Reviewer right: a failure in the type/length read or the range check returns at 575-583 before any field of the node is set, so the old claim that tl_data_contents is always set to NULL on failure was wrong. Not read: read_octets_or_minus1.

name: process_k5beta7_princ
prose: Static loader for one principal record of a kdb5_util "beta 7" dump (dump.c:598-790). It callocs a database entry, returning 1 at once if that fails. It increments *linenop (read_string can add to it), reads five size tokens with fscanf, and returns -1 after cleanup when fscanf returns EOF; any other mismatch or invalid size (name length above UINT_MAX/2, tl_data count above UINT16_MAX, key count above INT16_MAX, extra data size above UINT16_MAX) prints a message through load_err and goes to fail, while memory allocation failures for the name, the tl_data list and the key array go to fail without printing. It reads and parses the principal name (com_err message on parse failure), reads the eight attribute fields into the entry and sets the load mask, reads the tagged data through process_tl_data and, for KRB5_TL_KADM_DATA items, decodes the policy information to set mask bits, reads each key's version, kvno, types, lengths and contents (messages through load_err for unsupported versions, bad kvno or lengths and read errors), reads the extra data, reads the record end, and stores the entry with krb5_db_put_principal (failure: com_err message and fail). On success it prints the principal name when verbose and sets the result 0. Every path after the allocation reaches the cleanup code, which frees the key array copy, the name and the entry with krb5_db_free_principal; the function returns 0 on success, 1 on the failure paths (the fail label sets the result to 1) and -1 at EOF. A read_octets_or_minus1 failure inside, including an allocation failure there, is reported through load_err by this function (it prints "cannot read ..." messages), so not all allocation failures are silent.

name: kdb5_purge_mkeys
prose: The kdb5_util purge_mkeys command (kdb5_mkey.c:1004-1287; the real name is kdb5_purge_mkeys), returning void and reporting failures by incrementing the global exit_status. It first checks that the master key list is initialised (krb5_db_mkey_list_alias non-NULL); otherwise it prints an error, increments exit_status and returns. It parses the options -f (force), -n (dry run, which implies force) and -v (verbose) with getopt; an unknown option calls usage() and returns. It fetches the master key principal entry (failure: message, exit_status++, cleanup). Unless force is set it asks for confirmation and, if fgets returns NULL or the answer is not exactly "yes\n", increments exit_status and returns silently. If the entry has a single key version it returns (with a notice only if verbose, and without incrementing exit_status). Otherwise it allocates an array of the key versions (ENOMEM: message and exit_status++), records each version's kvno and calls krb5_db_iterate with find_mkvnos_in_use to count their use (failure: message, exit_status++). It then prints the versions that are unused (use_count 0); an unused kvno equal to master_kvno gives a KRB5_KDB_STORED_MKEY_NOTCURRENT message and exit_status++ and stops. If all versions are in use it prints "All keys in use, nothing purged." and returns without changing exit_status; in dry-run mode it prints how many would be purged and returns without modifying anything. Otherwise it looks up the active-kvno list and the mkey_aux list (failures: message, exit_status++), allocates a new key_data array for the versions in use (on failure it reports ENOMEM, with master_entry->key_data already set to NULL by the failed malloc assignment and the old array no longer referenced from the entry), moves the in-use keys into it, removes the list entries of the purged versions, frees the old key data and array, and calls krb5_dbe_update_actkvno, krb5_dbe_update_mkey_aux, krb5_timeofday and krb5_dbe_update_mod_princ_data (each failure reports a message, increments exit_status and returns without writing the database), sets the KEY_DATA and TL_DATA mask bits and writes the entry with krb5_db_put_principal (failure: message, exit_status++), printing "N key(s) purged." on success. Cleanup frees the entry, the kvno array and both lists.

name: do_iprop
prose: Incremental propagation loop of kpropd (kpropd.c:634-1003). It takes no arguments and uses the globals kpropd_context, realm, params, db_args, keytab_path, runonce and debug. It gets the primary's kiprop service name, builds and unparses the local kiprop service principal (any failure prints a message and goes to done), then initialises kadm5 with the keytab (label reinit). A kadm5 initialisation failure does not return: KADM5_RPC_ERROR frees any handle, sleeps with an exponential backoff and jumps back to reinit; other failures do the same after a message, except that KADM5_BAD_CLIENT_PARAMS and KADM5_BAD_SERVER_PARAMS call usage() first, which normally exits the process. After a successful initialisation it loops: it reads the local update log header (failure: message, done), calls iprop_get_updates_1; a NULL result destroys the handle and jumps to reinit. By the result code it handles UPDATE_FULL_RESYNC_NEEDED (requesting a full resync with full_resync unless one was requested within iprop_resync_timeout; a failed RPC reinitialises; UPDATE_PERM_DENIED and UPDATE_ERROR go to error and then done), UPDATE_OK (ulog_replay of the updates, only logging a failure), UPDATE_PERM_DENIED and UPDATE_ERROR (go to error), UPDATE_BUSY (backoff counter), UPDATE_NIL and unknown results (reset counters). If runonce is 1 and the result was not UPDATE_FULL_RESYNC_NEEDED it goes to done; otherwise it sleeps for the backoff time or the poll interval and repeats. At done it frees the service strings, principal and default realm, destroys the kadm5 handle, calls krb5_db_fini, ulog_fini and krb5_free_context(kpropd_context) (so the context is unusable afterwards) and returns 0 if runonce equals 1 and 1 otherwise, whether or not an error occurred. With runonce not equal to 1 it therefore returns 1 only after one of the error exits (it does not return on the normal polling path).

Reviewer 2 right (kadm5 initialisation failures retry via reinit, or usage() exits, 699-740); reviewer 1 mixed (the old formal contract was weaker, now empty); reviewer 3 mixed: the return value is (runonce == 1) ? 0 : 1 at 1002, neither "retval" nor "1 on every error path": with runonce equal to 1 an error exit returns 0.

name: process_stream_connection_read
prose: Verto read-event callback for a TCP connection of the KDC/kadmind network server (net-server.c:1359-1454). It gets the struct connection from the event's private data. If fewer than 4 bytes of the length prefix have been read it reads the missing prefix bytes; a read error or EOF goes to kill_tcp_connection, which deletes the event (freeing the connection and closing the socket through the event's private data). A short read just advances conn->offset and returns with the event still active. Once 4 bytes are present it takes msglen from them; if msglen is larger than bufsiz - 4 it logs, builds a FIELD_TOOLONG error response (failure: log and kill_tcp_connection), calls prepare_for_dispatch (which allocates a tcp_dispatch_state, detaches the connection and socket from the event, removes and deletes the event; if the allocation fails it frees the response and goes to kill_tcp_connection) and then calls process_stream_response with that response. process_stream_response does not delete the event: it stores the response, and either queues a write event for the connection (then frees the state) or, if the response is missing, there was an error code or the write event could not be made, decrements stream_data_counter, frees the connection, closes the socket and frees the state. If the length prefix is complete and within bounds the function returns and waits for the next event. If the prefix was already complete it reads the rest of the message (msglen - (offset - 4) bytes); read error or EOF kill the connection, a partial read advances the offset and returns with the event active, and a complete message calls prepare_for_dispatch (failure: kill_tcp_connection), sets the request to the buffer after the prefix, calls getsockname for the local address and dispatches the request asynchronously with process_stream_response as callback; if getsockname fails after prepare_for_dispatch has already deleted the event and detached the connection, the code still goes to kill_tcp_connection and calls verto_del(ev) again on that event, and the state and connection are not freed here.

Reviewer 1 right (partial reads return with the event active, 1387-1388 and 1427-1429); reviewer 2 right (prepare_for_dispatch deletes the event at 1353-1355 before process_stream_response runs, and process_stream_response does not delete it).

name: generic_gss_copy_oid_set
prose: Makes a deep copy of a GSS OID set (oid_ops.c:497-550; the real name is generic_gss_copy_oid_set). If minor_status is non-NULL it sets *minor_status to 0, and this is the only value it stores there (the release on the error path uses a local variable). If new_oidset is non-NULL it sets *new_oidset to GSS_C_NO_OID_SET. It returns GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ if oidset is GSS_C_NO_OID_SET and GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_WRITE if new_oidset is NULL, in both cases without allocating anything. Otherwise it callocs a set descriptor, callocs an array of oidset->count element descriptors (a zero count is passed to calloc as is), and for each element mallocs in->length bytes and copies them with memcpy, setting the element length. If any allocation fails it sets the result to GSS_S_FAILURE and releases the partial copy with generic_gss_release_oid_set (*new_oidset then stays GSS_C_NO_OID_SET). On success it stores the copy in *new_oidset and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE; the caller releases it with gss_release_oid_set.

name: shsUpdate
prose: Absorbs count bytes from buffer into the SHA-1 state shsInfo (shs.c:246-333; the slice began mid-function). It first adds count << 3 (the number of bits) to shsInfo->countLo, masks it to 32 bits, increments countHi on carry and adds count >> 29 to countHi, so countLo and countHi hold the total number of bits processed, not bytes. It computes how many bytes were already buffered from the old low count ((countLo >> 3) & 0x3F). If some bytes are buffered it completes the partial 32-bit word and the remaining words of the 16-word block data array from buffer in big-endian order (when buffer has fewer bytes than needed it stores what remains, zero-padding the last word, and sets count to 0), and calls SHSTransform(digest, data) when count was large enough to fill the block. It then processes every remaining full 64-byte (SHS_DATASIZE) chunk of buffer by loading it big-endian into data and calling SHSTransform. Any remaining bytes (fewer than 64) are loaded into the start of data as big-endian words, with the last partial word zero-padded, and stay buffered. buffer is only read; the function returns void. When count is 0 no bytes are read.
note: shs.c:246-330 read (the last lines 331-333 that close the function were not shown). Reviewer right: countLo and countHi are updated with count << 3 (255) so they are totals in bits, not bytes.

name: kg_accept_krb5
prose: Accepts a Kerberos GSS security context (accept_sec_context.c:667-1246). On entry it initialises the Kerberos context (failure: *minor_status = code, GSS_S_FAILURE), clears *src_name, *mech_type, *delegated_cred_handle and the output token, and uses a default acceptor credential when verifier_cred_handle is GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL. It resolves the credential with kg_cred_resolve, requires its usage to be GSS_C_ACCEPT or GSS_C_BOTH (otherwise GSS_S_NO_CRED), and parses the token header with parse_init_token. A token with a wrong token id gives GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with minor KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_MSG_TYPE; a malformed header (G_BAD_TOK_HEADER) is not rejected: the whole input is treated as a raw AP-REQ without the GSS framing (no_encap); any other parse error gives GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN. It decodes the AP-REQ (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), sets up an auth context (replay cache, addresses, permitted enctypes), calls krb5_rd_req_decoded (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), and then, in the part I did not read line by line (835-1060), checks the authenticator and channel bindings, builds the security context and delegated credential, and decides the flags. With mutual authentication it builds an AP-REP token; for DCE-style contexts it stores the context in *context_handle with established cleared, returns the AP-REP in output_token and returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED; otherwise the context is established, the AP-REP token is built in output_token (empty without mutual authentication) and the function sets the optional outputs (source name copy, mech type, lifetime, flags, delegated credential) and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with *minor_status 0 and *context_handle set to the new context. On the fail path a failure (any result other than COMPLETE, or CONTINUE_NEEDED without the MSG_TYPE code) deletes the partially built context, delegated credential, token and name, stores code in *minor_status, and, when a credential and a decoded request exist and mutual authentication was requested (by the flags or the request) or the result was CONTINUE_NEEDED, it builds a KRB-ERROR token and puts it in output_token, so output_token is not always empty on error. The done label frees the decoded request, unlocks the credential lock, releases a default credential and frees the Kerberos context unless it was handed to the new security context. *context_handle is set only on COMPLETE or the DCE CONTINUE_NEEDED return.
note: Partly read: accept_sec_context.c:667-835 and 1060-1246 in full (comments skipped); lines 835-1060 (authenticator, channel bindings, delegation, context construction) were only checked through a goto fail skeleton. Reviewer 1 right (the CONTINUE_NEEDED path for a wrong token id, 764-768); reviewer 2 right (G_BAD_TOK_HEADER makes the input a raw AP-REQ rather than a DEFECTIVE_TOKEN error, 769-773). The old statement that output_token stays empty on every error path is wrong because of the KRB-ERROR token built at 1193-1231.

name: kg_cred_resolve
prose: Resolves the name and ccache of a krb5 GSS credential (acquire_cred.c:965-1053). It sets *minor_status = 0 and calls krb5_gss_validate_cred_1 on cred_handle; a non-zero result is returned unchanged (the validate function takes the credential lock on success; its failure behaviour was not read). With the lock held, an accept credential, or any credential that already has a name, is returned as GSS_S_COMPLETE without changing its name or ccache. Otherwise (an initiator credential without a name) it resolves them: if target_name is given it selects a cache for it with krb5_cc_select (KRB5_CC_NOTFOUND is tolerated), sets cred->name from the selected principal and scans the selected ccache; if the name is still unset it opens the default ccache, scans it (KRB5_FCC_NOFILE closes the cache and clears it, other errors fail); if the name is still unset it tries the client keytab (failure becomes KG_EMPTY_CCACHE); if a name now exists but there is no ccache it gets one with get_cache_for_name; then it calls maybe_get_initial_cred and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with the credential lock still held. Any of the failing steps goes to kerr, which unlocks the credential, saves the error info, sets *minor_status to the error code and returns GSS_S_NO_CRED.

Reviewer 1 right (for GSS_C_ACCEPT or an already named credential the name and ccache are not resolved, 982-983); reviewer 2 wrong: the kerr path sets *minor_status to the error code (1051), not 0. Not read: krb5_gss_validate_cred_1, scan_ccache, get_cache_for_name, maybe_get_initial_cred.

name: krb5_gss_init_sec_context_ext
prose: Kerberos mechanism's gss_init_sec_context (init_sec_context.c:871-988, which calls the static helpers kg_new_connection at 461-688 and mutual_auth at 695-868, the two of which make up this slice; the packet name krb5_gss_init_sec_context was an inference). For a new context (*context_handle is GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT) it initialises a Kerberos context and syncs the ccache name (failure: GSS_S_FAILURE), otherwise it uses the context saved in the existing GSS context. It clears the output token and *actual_mech_type, maps mech_type (NULL OID, krb5, old krb5, wrong krb5 or iakerb OIDs are accepted, anything else gives GSS_S_BAD_MECH with minor 0 after freeing a context it created). For a first call it uses the default credential if none was passed, resolves it with kg_cred_resolve (errors returned with the context freed) and calls kg_new_connection with the credential lock held. kg_new_connection returns GSS_S_NO_CRED (minor 0) when the credential cannot initiate and GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN (minor 0) when an input token of non-zero length is given on the first call; it allocates a context (ENOMEM gives GSS_S_FAILURE), sets flags from req_flags (GSS_C_DCE_STYLE adds GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG; the delegation policy flag is handled), computes the end time, duplicates the local and target names, gets service credentials with get_credentials, builds the AP-REQ with make_ap_req_v1 (KRB5_FCC_NOFILE, KRB5_CC_NOTFOUND and KG_EMPTY_CCACHE give GSS_S_NO_CRED; KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED gives GSS_S_CREDENTIALS_EXPIRED; other failures GSS_S_FAILURE with *minor_status set to the code), creates the subkeys, and on success stores the context in *context_handle and the AP-REQ in *output_token, sets *ret_flags, *time_rec and *actual_mech_type when requested, and returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED with the context not established when GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG is set (including DCE style) or GSS_S_COMPLETE with it established otherwise; on failure it frees the partial context and leaves *context_handle unchanged. For a later call it runs mutual_auth, which fails with GSS_S_FAILURE (code KG_CONTEXT_ESTABLISHED) if the context is already established or has no mutual flag, GSS_S_BAD_NAME if the target name does not match, and GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN for a missing input token (the last two after deleting the context), returns GSS_S_DEFECTIVE_TOKEN with minor 0 for a bad token header or a token type other than AP-REP or error without deleting the context, passes on a KRB-ERROR token's code, verifies the AP-REP with krb5_rd_rep (one retry with the user-to-user key), sets the receive sequence and the acceptor subkey when present, builds a DCE-style reply when requested, marks the context established, sets ret_flags, time_rec and actual_mech_type when requested and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with minor 0. All other failures of mutual_auth delete the context (setting *context_handle to GSS_C_NO_CONTEXT) and return GSS_S_FAILURE with the Kerberos code in *minor_status, including the established/no-mutual-flag failure (the fail label deletes the context although a comment says the arguments are unchanged). The mutex of the credential is released after the first-call helper returns.
note: init_sec_context.c:461-988 read (comments skipped). Reviewer right (DCE style sets the mutual flag, 554-555, so the first call returns GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED although the caller did not request mutual authentication). The previous prose also said *context_handle is unchanged on every first-call failure, which holds for kg_new_connection but mutual_auth failures delete the context.

name: kg_ctx_internalize
prose: Rebuilds a krb5 GSS security context from its serialised form (ser_sctx.c:484-692; the real name is kg_ctx_internalize). Arguments: the krb5 context, the output pointer argp, and *buffer and *lenremain for the input position and remaining length. It reads a 32-bit tag; if the read fails or the tag is not KG_CONTEXT the result is EINVAL and nothing else happens. Otherwise the result starts as ENOMEM, and it stays ENOMEM both when the remaining length is smaller than the fixed header size (17 int32s, two int64s and the seed) and when allocating the context fails, in which case nothing is allocated and *argp is not set. With enough input it zeroes a new context and unpacks the fixed fields (the results of many int32 and byte unpacks are not checked), then the two sequence numbers (failure frees the context and returns that error), then in order the mechanism OID, the two principals as names, the subkey, enc and seq keys, the sequence state (an EINVAL from these optional parts means the part is absent and is turned into success), the krb5 context, the auth context, proto, cksumtype, the acceptor subkey (EINVAL again tolerated), its checksum type, cred_rcache, and an authdata array (calloc failure gives ENOMEM) and the initiator name's authdata context (a missing initiator name gives EINVAL; an EINVAL from the authdata context is tolerated). It finally reads the trailer tag, which must equal KG_CONTEXT or the result is EINVAL. On success it advances *buffer and *lenremain past the trailer, stores the new context in *argp (the caller owns it) and returns 0. On a failure after the allocation it frees the seq, enc and subkey keys, the names there and here and the context structure, and returns the error with *argp, *buffer and *lenremain unchanged; the acceptor subkey, mech OID, k5 context, auth context and authdata entries are not freed.

The previous prose said that with too few bytes it returns 0 without setting *argp; the code sets kret = ENOMEM at 508 before the length test, so that case returns ENOMEM (511-515 and 691). Fixed under the real name; no reviewer claim beyond the mechanical name rejection.

name: gss_add_cred_from
prose: GSS mechglue function (g_acquire_cred.c:386-582) that adds a credential for one mechanism to a union credential. It first calls val_add_cred_args; any non-COMPLETE status from it is returned. It selects the mechanism with gssint_select_mech_type (its failure is returned) and looks up the mechanism: GSS_S_BAD_MECH if none, GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE if it has no gss_acquire_cred, and GSS_S_DUPLICATE_ELEMENT if the input credential already has a credential for that mechanism; these returns do not set *minor_status in this function. If there is no input credential it allocates an empty union credential (GSS_S_FAILURE if malloc fails); if there is an input and output_cred_handle is non-NULL it works on a copy made with copy_union_cred (failure returned); with output_cred_handle NULL it modifies the input union credential itself. It converts desired_name to the mechanism's internal name (using the union name's own mech name when it matches, otherwise importing; failure gives GSS_S_BAD_NAME), picks the requested time from cred_usage, gets the public OID of the mechanism, and acquires the mechanism credential with gss_acquire_cred_from when the mechanism has it, or with gss_acquire_cred when cred_store is GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, otherwise it fails with GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE; a mechanism error status is mapped with map_error and handled as a failure. It then grows the union credential's mechs_array and cred_array with realloc (GSS_S_FAILURE on failure; the arrays can stay reallocated with the count unchanged), writes *acceptor_time_rec and *initiator_time_rec when requested and the usage covers them, copies the mechanism OID, fills *actual_mechs when requested (an error goes to the failure path), stores the new credential, increments the count and, if output_cred_handle is non-NULL, stores the union credential there. On success it releases a name it imported and returns GSS_S_COMPLETE. The failure path releases the mechanism credential, the imported internal name, and, when output_cred_handle is non-NULL, the working union credential, frees the OID buffer and returns the status; however the malloc failure of the OID buffer (line 536-538) jumps to this path with status still holding the GSS_S_COMPLETE value left by the successful acquire, so that case returns GSS_S_COMPLETE even though nothing was added and the new credential was released.

Reviewer 1 right (duplicate element, UNAVAILABLE and cred_store requirements are not in the old preconditions); reviewer 2 right (BAD_MECH, UNAVAILABLE, DUPLICATE_ELEMENT return without setting *minor_status in this function, 427-436).

name: addConfigEntry
prose: Static function in g_initialize.c (lines 1486-1618; the real name is addConfigEntry) that registers one mechanism read from the GSS configuration; the caller is expected to hold the mechanism-list lock. Parameters are the mechanism name oidStr, its dotted OID string oid, the library sharedLib, and the optional kernMod, modOptions and modType. It returns void and silently leaves the list unchanged if oid or oidStr is NULL, if the OID string cannot be converted by generic_gss_str_to_oid, if an entry for that OID already has a loaded mech (searchMechList finds an entry with aMech->mech set; the converted OID is released), or if sharedLib is an empty string (the OID is released); sharedLib itself is dereferenced without a NULL check. The library path is sharedLib if it starts with '/' and otherwise MECH_LIB_PREFIX followed by sharedLib (non-Windows, written with snprintf into a fixed buffer). If an entry for the OID exists but is not loaded it frees and clears its kmodName and optionStr, replaces uLibName with a copy of the path when strdup succeeds, sets kmodName and optionStr to copies of kernMod and modOptions when those are non-NULL (a strdup failure leaves them NULL), releases the converted OID and returns; is_interposer is not changed there. Otherwise it callocs a new entry (on failure the OID is released and nothing changes), stores the converted OID in it, copies the path and the name (if either strdup fails it frees what was allocated, the OID and the entry and returns), copies kernMod and modOptions when non-NULL without checking the strdup results, sets is_interposer when modType is "interposer", appends the entry at the tail of the list and makes it the head if the list was empty.
note: g_initialize.c:1486-1618 read in full, comments skipped. Reviewer wrong: in the existing-entry path kmodName and optionStr are freed and set to NULL unconditionally at 1548-1556, before they are set again from kernMod and modOptions, so they are cleared when kernMod or modOptions is absent. Fixed under the real name; the packet had marked it dropped.

name: gss_store_cred_into
prose: GSS mechglue function (g_store_cred.c:108-238) that stores the credentials of a union credential with the mechanisms' credential stores, optionally into a given cred_store. It first calls val_store_cred_args and returns any non-COMPLETE status from it (the argument checks live there; they were not read), then sets *cred_usage_stored (when non-NULL) to GSS_C_BOTH and starts with GSS_S_FAILURE. With a desired_mech it selects the mechanism with gssint_select_mech_type (a non-COMPLETE result is returned) and gets its interface, returning GSS_S_BAD_MECH if there is none. If the mechanism has no gss_store_cred_into and cred_store is not GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, or has neither gss_store_cred nor gss_store_cred_into, it returns major_status at that point, which holds the value of the successful gssint_select_mech_type call, GSS_S_COMPLETE, so nothing is stored but success is reported. Otherwise it fetches the mechanism's credential (GSS_S_NO_CRED if the union credential has none) and stores it through store_cred_fallback (the mechanism's gss_store_cred_into, or gss_store_cred when cred_store is GSS_C_NO_CRED_STORE, otherwise GSS_S_UNAVAILABLE), mapping the mechanism error with map_error on failure, and returns that status with elements_stored and cred_usage_stored filled in by the mechanism. Without a desired_mech it sets *minor_status to 0 and tries every mechanism element of the union credential, skipping elements that lack a mechanism interface, lack the needed store function or have no credential; for each attempted element a failure is mapped and the loop continues, and a success adds the mechanism's OID to *elements_stored when elements_stored is non-NULL (creating the empty set first; an error from these set operations is returned at once). The final result is the status of the last attempted element (GSS_S_COMPLETE when that one succeeded even if an earlier one failed, GSS_S_FAILURE if none was attempted).

Reviewer 1 right (a mechanism lacking the store entry points returns GSS_S_COMPLETE without storing, 155-161, because major_status holds the select result); reviewer 2 wrong for the same reason: the code does not return GSS_S_FAILURE there, since line 145 overwrote the initial FAILURE value.

name: mech_init
prose: Static function in negoex_ctx.c (lines 276-348) used by the NegoEx initiator to start the first available mechanism. It first sets output_token to empty. If ctx->negoex_step is 1 and the environment variable NEGOEX_NO_OPTIMISTIC_TOKEN is set (checked with secure_getenv) it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE at once with the empty token and no mechanism started. If the mechanism list is empty it sets *minor to ERR_NEGOEX_NO_AVAILABLE_MECHS and returns GSS_S_FAILURE (this test comes after the environment check). It takes the first mechanism and, if a CHALLENGE exchange message exists whose scheme equals that mechanism's scheme, uses its token as the input token; if that first mechanism is already complete it returns GSS_S_COMPLETE with an empty output token. Otherwise it loops over the list: it calls gss_init_sec_context for the first mechanism with the input token, marks it complete when the result is GSS_S_COMPLETE, and if the result is not a GSS error returns get_session_keys(minor, mech) (so the result of that call is what the caller sees). On a GSS error it records the major and minor codes of the first mechanism tried, deletes the failed mechanism with negoex_delete_auth_mech, clears the input token (so the CHALLENGE token is only given to the first mechanism) and tries the next one. When all mechanisms have been deleted the loop ends and it returns the first mechanism's major code with *minor set to its minor code.

name: ulog_replay
prose: Replays the update entries received by an incremental propagation client into the local database and update log (kdb_log.c:400-480; the slice started inside this function). INIT_ULOG(context) sets up the log context first (not read). It opens the database read-write with krb5_db_open and returns that error if it fails; the database stays open afterwards. It then loops i from 0 to the number of updates in incr_ret using a pointer upd that starts at the first entry. For an entry whose kdb_commit is false it executes continue without advancing upd, so the next iteration examines the same entry again; if the first entry is uncommitted the loop therefore skips all later entries too. For a committed entry it deletes the principal (the name copied and parsed; krb5int_delete_principal_no_log; KRB5_KDB_NOENTRY is treated as success) when kdb_deleted is set, otherwise converts the entry with ulog_conv_2dbentry and stores it with krb5int_put_principal_no_log and frees it; any error goes to cleanup. It then takes the exclusive ulog lock; if the log header already has entries (kdb_num != 0) and the update's serial number is not kdb_last_sno + 1 it resets the ulog; it stores the update with store_update, releases the lock, and on error goes to cleanup; otherwise it advances upd. At cleanup, on any error it calls ulog_init_header (which resets the ulog under the lock); whether or not there was an error it frees the whole update array with ulog_free_entries when it is non-NULL, and returns retval, which is 0 when all iterations ended without error.

The old prose said the update array is freed only on error; it is freed at 477-478 on every path after the database was opened.

name: ulog_map
prose: Opens and maps the KDC update log file (kdb_log.c:500-577; the real name is ulog_map and the packet slice held it only partly). It creates a log context with create_log_context; if that returns NULL it returns ENOMEM without cleanup. If stat(logname) fails it opens the file with O_RDWR|O_CREAT and mode 0600 and extends it with extend_file_to to sizeof(kdb_hlog_t) + ulogentries * ULOG_BLOCK; if stat succeeds it opens the existing file O_RDWR. A failed open returns errno (through cleanup). It maps MAXLOGLEN bytes of the file read-write and shared (a failed mmap returns errno), stores the mapping and ulogentries in the log context, and takes the exclusive ulog lock (failure returned). If the header magic is not KDB_ULOG_HDR_MAGIC it returns KRB5_LOG_CORRUPT when the magic is non-zero, or resets the log when it is zero. If the log is non-empty and kdb_num exceeds ulogentries or the first or last serial number fails check_sno it resets the log. If kdb_num differs from ulogentries it extends the file to sizeof(kdb_hlog_t) + ulogentries * ulog->kdb_block (failure returned). At cleanup it releases the lock if it was taken and, when an error occurred, calls ulog_fini; it returns the error code or 0. On success the log context, the mapping and the file descriptor stay in place for later use.

name: kr_remote_equals
prose: Tests whether the remote RADIUS server rr matches the given addrinfo and shared secret (krad remote.c:503-540). It returns FALSE if strcmp(rr->secret, secret) differs, or if ai_addrlen, ai_family, ai_socktype, ai_protocol or ai_flags differ between info and rr->info. It then compares the socket address bytes with memcmp over info->ai_addrlen; if they differ it returns FALSE unless the family is AF_UNIX, in which case it compares the two sun_path strings with strncmp over the size of sun_path and returns FALSE if they differ (this allows for uninitialised bytes after the path in AF_UNIX addresses). Otherwise it returns TRUE. It has no side effects.

name: begin_get_tgt
prose: Static function in get_creds.c (lines 987-1031; the slice cut the head) that starts obtaining the TGT needed for a TGS exchange. It sets ctx->state to STATE_GET_TGT. It treats the service as local when ctx->start_realm equals ctx->server->realm. If it is not local it looks for a cached TGT for the server's realm with get_cached_tgt; an error is returned immediately (ctx->cur_tgt is then unchanged and may still hold an earlier non-local TGT); if one is found it replaces ctx->cur_tgt with it (freeing the old one) and returns end_get_tgt(context, ctx). Otherwise it frees ctx->cur_tgt, sets it to NULL and fetches the cached local TGT with get_cached_local_tgt into ctx->cur_tgt (error returned, with cur_tgt NULL or whatever that callee left). If the service is local it returns end_get_tgt. Otherwise it builds the realm path with init_realm_path (error returned, with ctx->cur_tgt holding the local TGT), frees and clears ctx->realms_seen, and returns get_tgt_request(context, ctx), which generates the first request towards the realm and does not call end_get_tgt here. The return value is 0 or the first error code of those calls (or the result of end_get_tgt or get_tgt_request).

name: process_pa_data
prose: Static function in preauth2.c (lines 648-729) that runs the client preauth modules over the padata received from the KDC. It makes two passes over in_pa_list (the first, real = 0, for informational padata; the second, real = 1, for real mechanisms). For each entry it skips it when it is a real pass and the type is not allowed (pa_type_allowed), when no module handles the type, when the module's real/informational class differs from the pass, and in the real pass when the type has failed before. It then calls clpreauth_process, which may produce an output list mod_pa. If mod_pa is non-NULL it appends it with grow_pa_list to *out_pa_list (updating *out_pa_list_size) and frees the array; if the append fails it frees mod_pa with krb5_free_pa_data and returns the error from grow_pa_list. Note that this append assignment overwrites ret, so the module's own return code is replaced by 0 whenever it produced output padata and the append succeeded, which masks a module error (including KRB5_LIBOS_PWDINTR) in that case. If ret is KRB5_LIBOS_PWDINTR it returns it at once. If ret is 0 in the real pass it sets *out_type to the entry's type and returns 0. A failed real entry saves the error context for the first failure and calls k5_preauth_note_failed (ret is replaced by its result and returned if non-zero). After both passes, if must_preauth is true it returns KRB5_PREAUTH_FAILED (wrapping the saved error message when one was saved). If must_preauth is false it returns the value of ret left by the last module call or note_failed (0 if none ran), which for informational entries is that module's own return code. It clears the saved error info on exit.

Reviewer 1 right (KRB5_LIBOS_PWDINTR returns at once, 697-698, and with must_preauth false the value left in ret, not the first saved error, is returned); reviewer 2 right (the grow_pa_list assignment at 689 overwrites ret so a module's error can be masked).

name: k5_privsafe_check_seqnum
prose: Checks the received sequence number in_seq of a KRB-PRIV or KRB-SAFE message against the expected number ac->remote_seq_number (privsafe.c:225-304; the packet's name seq_check and the slice, which also contains k5_privsafe_check_addrs, point to this function). The context argument is unused. It returns a krb5_boolean. If KRB5_AUTH_CONN_SANE_SEQ is set it returns whether in_seq equals the expected number, with no flag change. Otherwise, when in_seq is in 0xFF800000..0xFFFFFFFF, it returns true for an exact match if the expected number is also in that range, or if KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ is not set; else it calls chk_heimdal_seqnum(exp_seq, in_seq) (which accepts the three Heimdal wrap-around patterns for an expected value in 0x80..0xFF, 0x8000..0xFFFF or 0x800000..0xFFFFFF) and, if that accepts, sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ and returns true; otherwise it returns false. For any other in_seq, an exact match returns true, and also sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_SANE_SEQ when the expected number is in one of the three ambiguous Heimdal ranges (masks 0xFFFFFF80 = 0x80, 0xFFFF8000 = 0x8000, 0xFF800000 = 0x800000). If the expected number is 0 and KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ is not yet set, an in_seq of 0x100, 0x10000 or 0x1000000 sets KRB5_AUTH_CONN_HEIMDAL_SEQ and returns true (the assignment to the local exp_seq has no effect on ac->remote_seq_number), and any other in_seq returns false. Everything else returns false.

name: rd_req_decoded_opt
prose: Static worker in rd_req_dec.c (lines 473-787; the real name is rd_req_decoded_opt and the packet slice is its middle) behind krb5_rd_req_decoded, verifying an already decoded AP-REQ req for the accepting principal server with an optional keytab; check_valid_flag selects whether invalid-flag checking and authdata verification are done. Arguments include *auth_context (must be initialised), optional *ap_req_options and **ticket outputs. It first decrypts the ticket's encrypted part: with a key in the auth context (user-to-user) it decrypts with it, frees that key and clears the field (keeping the key contents in a local decrypt_key when check_valid_flag is set); otherwise it uses decrypt_ticket with the keytab and takes the server from the ticket. Failures go to cleanup with their error. It decrypts the authenticator, returns KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BADMATCH if the authenticator's client differs from the ticket's client, and KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_BADADDR if the auth context has a remote address that is not in the ticket's address list. If there is no replay cache and KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_DO_TIME is set it opens the default one (error returned). It then applies the cross-realm policy (under the default build: when the ticket's transit policy was not checked and its transited field is non-empty, krb5_check_transited_list; the other two build variants return KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_ILL_CR_TKT for non-empty transit or a foreign realm) and stores the authenticator in the replay cache with k5_rc_store when a cache exists (error returned). It then checks the ticket times (krb5int_validate_times) and the clock skew of the authenticator time; with check_valid_flag it also returns KRB5KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_INVALID for an invalid ticket, initialises the authdata context and verifies the authdata. It decodes the RFC 4537 etype list from the authenticator, builds the desired etype list (adding the authenticator subkey's and the ticket session key's enctype; ENOMEM on allocation failure), obtains the permitted enctypes unless KRB5_AUTH_CONTEXT_PERMIT_ALL is set, and negotiates the enctype into negotiated_etype (failure returned). It sets remote_seq_number from the authenticator, creates recv_subkey and send_subkey from the authenticator subkey when present (freeing the recv key if the send key creation fails, else setting both to NULL), creates the session key reference in (*auth_context)->key, and XORs local_seq_number with remote_seq_number when mutual authentication was not requested and the remote number is non-zero. If ticket is non-NULL it copies the ticket (error returned). If ap_req_options is non-NULL it sets it to req->ap_options & AP_OPTS_WIRE_MASK, ORed with AP_OPTS_ETYPE_NEGOTIATION when an RFC 4537 list was present and AP_OPTS_USE_SUBKEY when the negotiated enctype differs from the key's enctype. It returns 0 on success. Cleanup frees desired_etypes, a permitted list obtained locally, and the local decrypt_key contents when check_valid_flag is set; on a failure the auth context may keep fields set before the failing step (keys already created are not released).

name: k5_internalize_auth_context
prose: Rebuilds a krb5 auth context from its serialised form (ser_actx.c:250-397; the real name is k5_internalize_auth_context). Arguments: the output pointer argp and *buffer and *lenremain as input position and remaining length. It reads a 32-bit tag; if the read fails or the tag is not KV5M_AUTH_CONTEXT the result is EINVAL and nothing is allocated. Otherwise the result starts as ENOMEM; it stays ENOMEM if fewer than 5 int32s remain or the calloc of the context fails (argp is then not set). With enough input it unpacks the flags, the remote and local sequence numbers and the two checksum types (the results of these unpacks are not checked), then the cstate length and bytes (alloc_data and unpack errors propagate), then a tag-driven sequence of optional parts, each present only when its tag matches: remote address, remote port, local address, local port, key, send subkey, and, if the next tag is TOKEN_RSKBLOCK, the receive subkey (otherwise the tag bytes it consumed are put back by moving the position back four bytes). It then reads the authenticator (an EINVAL from k5_internalize_authenticator is turned into success, i.e. an absent authenticator) and the trailing tag, which must be KV5M_AUTH_CONTEXT or the result is EINVAL. On success it advances *buffer and *lenremain past the trailer, sets the magic and stores the new context in *argp (the caller owns and frees it with krb5_auth_con_free); on any failure after allocation it frees the partly built context with krb5_auth_con_free and returns the error with *argp, *buffer and *lenremain unchanged.

name: start_connection
prose: Static helper in sendto_kdc.c (lines 885-990) that opens a non-blocking socket to the server in state->addr and registers it in selstate. It creates the socket (type from the transport); if socket() fails it returns -1 without touching state (no descriptor exists). It sets close-on-exec and non-blocking mode, and for TCP a zero linger. It calls connect: if that fails with an error other than EINPROGRESS or EWOULDBLOCK it closes the socket, sets state->state to FAILED (state->fd is not updated) and returns -2; EINPROGRESS or EWOULDBLOCK stores the socket in state->fd with state CONNECTING, and an immediate success stores it with state WRITING. If a callback_info is given it calls its callback with state->fd; on failure it closes the socket, sets state->fd to INVALID_SOCKET and state to FAILED and returns -3, otherwise the callback's buffer replaces the message. It then calls set_transport_message; on failure it closes state->fd, sets it to INVALID_SOCKET, state to FAILED and returns -4. For UDP it sends the initial datagram; a failed or short send closes the socket, sets fd INVALID_SOCKET and state FAILED and returns -5, and a successful send sets state READING. It then adds the descriptor to selstate with cm_add_fd; if that fails it closes the socket, sets fd INVALID_SOCKET and state FAILED and returns -1. Finally it registers the descriptor for writing when the state is CONNECTING or WRITING and for reading otherwise, and returns 0.
